subject: biology-hl
author: original (NevaIB)
title: Transport
bigPicture: Mass transport carries materials too far for diffusion. In animals, the heart pumps blood through arteries, capillaries and veins, each shaped for its job; in plants, transpiration pulls water up the xylem and phloem carries sugars from sources to sinks.

keyIdeas.cue: How are capillaries adapted for exchange?
keyIdeas.answer: Highly branched and narrow, giving a huge surface area close to every cell; walls one cell thick; some are fenestrated (with pores) where exchange must be fast, e.g. kidney, intestine.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you tell an artery from a vein in a micrograph?
keyIdeas.answer: Artery: thick wall relative to a small, round lumen. Vein: thin wall relative to a large, often irregular lumen.

Thick layers of smooth muscle and elastic tissue withstand high pressure; elastic fibres stretch with each pulse and recoil, keeping pressure up and evening out flow; muscle can narrow or widen the vessel.

keyIdeas.cue: How do you measure pulse rate?
keyIdeas.answer: Feel the radial (wrist) or carotid (neck) pulse with fingertips, count beats for 30 s and double it (or 60 s). Compare with a digital monitor.
Valves prevent backflow at low pressure; thin, flexible walls are squeezed by surrounding skeletal muscles to push blood back towards the heart.

keyIdeas.cue: What causes coronary occlusion and what happens?
keyIdeas.answer: Fatty plaques (atherosclerosis) narrow the coronary arteries; a clot may block them. Heart muscle beyond the blockage gets no O₂ and dies (heart attack). Epidemiological data show correlations with risk factors such as saturated fat, smoking and blood pressure, but correlation, even strong, does not prove cause.

keyIdeas.cue: How does water move from roots to leaves?
keyIdeas.answer: Water evaporates from leaf cell walls and is replaced by capillary action, creating tension (negative pressure) in the xylem. The tension pulls water up; cohesion between water molecules (hydrogen bonds) keeps the column continuous.
Dead, with no cell contents, and no end walls, so flow is unimpeded; lignified walls resist collapse under tension; pits let water move in and out sideways.

keyIdeas.cue: What does a dicot stem section show?
keyIdeas.answer: Epidermis outside, cortex, and vascular bundles in a ring: xylem towards the centre, phloem towards the outside. Annotate functions (support, water transport, sugar transport, protection).

keyIdeas.cue: What does a dicot root section show?
keyIdeas.answer: Epidermis (with root hairs), wide cortex, and a central vascular cylinder: xylem often in an X or star shape with phloem between its arms.

keyIdeas.cue: How is tissue fluid formed and reabsorbed?
keyIdeas.answer: High pressure at the arteriole end forces plasma out through capillary walls (pressure filtration). At the venule end pressure is lower, so most fluid drains back into the capillaries.

keyIdeas.cue: How do plasma and tissue fluid differ?
keyIdeas.answer: Tissue fluid is similar to plasma but has almost no large plasma proteins (too big to filter out). Cells take O₂, glucose and other nutrients from it and release CO₂ and wastes into it.

keyIdeas.cue: What happens to excess tissue fluid?
keyIdeas.answer: It drains into lymph ducts, which have thin walls with gaps and valves. Lymph returns to the blood circulation near the heart.
Bony fish: heart → gills → body → heart (one pass, low pressure to the body). Mammals: heart → lungs → heart → body → heart; the second pump restores high pressure for the body circuit.

keyIdeas.cue: How is the heart adapted to pump blood at pressure?
keyIdeas.answer: Cardiac muscle contracts without fatigue; the sinoatrial node (pacemaker) starts each beat; thin-walled atria pump to ventricles; thick-walled ventricles (left thickest) pump to arteries; atrioventricular and semilunar valves keep flow one way; the septum separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood; coronary vessels supply the muscle. Flow: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery; pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

keyIdeas.cue: Describe the cardiac cycle on the left side.
keyIdeas.answer: SA node fires; atria contract (atrial systole), pushing blood into the ventricles. Ventricles contract (ventricular systole): AV valve shuts when ventricle pressure exceeds atrium; semilunar valve opens when it exceeds aorta. Diastole: ventricle relaxes, semilunar valve shuts, AV valve opens and the heart refills. Systolic/diastolic pressure (e.g. 120/80 mmHg) are the peak and lowest arterial pressures.

Root cells actively pump mineral ions into the xylem; water follows by osmosis, creating positive pressure that pushes water up. Important when transpiration is low, e.g. high humidity or in spring before leaves open.

keyIdeas.cue: How are phloem sieve tubes and companion cells adapted?
keyIdeas.answer: Sieve tube elements have sieve plates, little cytoplasm, few organelles and no nucleus, so sap flows easily. Companion cells have many mitochondria to load sugars actively, and are linked to sieve tubes by plasmodesmata. Sugars are loaded at sources (leaves) and unloaded at sinks (roots, fruits).

keyTerms.def: The space inside a vessel through which blood flows.
Tension in xylem created by evaporation from leaves.
Attraction between water molecules via hydrogen bonds.
Fluid filtered from plasma that bathes cells.
Pacemaker in the right atrium that starts each heartbeat.
Movement of sap with sugars in phloem from source to sink.

workedExamples.title: Pulse rate
workedExamples.prompt: A student counts 19 radial pulses in 15 s. Calculate heart rate.
workedExamples.answer: 76 beats per minute (count for longer for accuracy).

workedExamples.title: Interpret a correlation
workedExamples.prompt: Countries with higher saturated fat intake have higher coronary heart disease rates (r = 0.85). Can you conclude saturated fat causes CHD?
steps: r = 0.85 is a strong positive correlation.
Other factors (smoking, exercise, wealth, diagnosis rates) may vary with fat intake.
workedExamples.answer: No: it supports the hypothesis but needs controlled or mechanistic evidence for causation.

misconceptions.wrong: Veins carry deoxygenated blood, arteries oxygenated.
misconceptions.right: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and pulmonary vein oxygenated.

misconceptions.wrong: Water is pushed up the xylem from the roots.
misconceptions.right: Mainly it is pulled up by tension from transpiration; root pressure helps only when transpiration is low.

misconceptions.wrong: The heart's valves are opened by muscles.
misconceptions.right: They open and close because of pressure differences.

misconceptions.wrong: Capillary walls are thin to let blood cells out.
misconceptions.right: They are thin for short diffusion distance; red cells stay inside.

misconceptions.wrong: Tissue fluid is the same as plasma.
misconceptions.right: It lacks most of the large plasma proteins.

practice.prompt: Distinguish between the structure of arteries and veins.
checkpoints: Veins: thin walls, wide lumen, valves

practice.prompt: Explain how water is transported from roots to leaves.
checkpoints: Adhesion/capillary action; lignified xylem withstands tension

practice.prompt: Evaluate the claim that high cholesterol intake causes coronary heart disease, using epidemiological data.
checkpoints: Confounding factors / need for controlled studies

practice.prompt: Explain the action of the heart valves during one cardiac cycle on the left side.
checkpoints: Ventricle pressure > atrium: AV valve closes
Ventricle pressure > aorta: semilunar valve opens
Diastole: semilunar valve closes, AV valve opens

practice.prompt: Outline how tissue fluid forms and returns to the blood.
checkpoints: High pressure at arteriole end filters plasma out
Lower pressure at venule end lets fluid return; excess into lymph
